source.verse_hash_method: SHA-256 of exact tab-separated Greek payload, retaining whitespace and variant markers.

notes: Paul distinguishes the holy commandment from sin, which exploits the commandment to deceive and kill.
The identity and life-setting of the first-person ‘I’ are disputed. The translation preserves Paul's present-tense conflict rather than assigning it to one doctrinal scheme.
‘Body of death’ is retained as Paul's severe bodily image, not reduced to an abstract problem.
vocabulary: Made of flesh; fleshly or mortal.
Take captive as a prisoner of war.

notes: The pinned Greek ends after ‘Christ Jesus’; it does not include the longer clause about walking according to the Spirit.
‘Sons’ retains the gendered Roman adoption and inheritance status; ‘children’ appears where the Greek changes terms.
The pinned text reads that ‘all things work together’; some witnesses explicitly name God as the one who works all things together.
Paul names persecution, hunger, exposure, danger, and killing as real harms. The claim is that none can separate believers from divine love, not that suffering is unreal.
vocabulary: Adoption as a son, carrying family status and inheritance rights.
Redemption or release secured at a cost.

notes: Paul's impossible-sounding wish to be accursed expresses anguish for his own Israelite kin; it is not a curse pronounced on them.
The compact Greek punctuation can connect ‘God blessed forever’ directly to the Messiah, as in the main text, or take it as a separate blessing of God.
The language of hatred, hardening, wrath, and vessels is translated directly. The passage's objections and unanswered pressures are not softened into a complete theological system.
‘Sons of the living God’ retains the gendered title in Hosea's quotation.
vocabulary: Accursed, devoted to destruction, or cut off.
Potter, one who shapes clay vessels.

notes: τέλος can mean end, goal, result, or culmination. ‘Culmination’ preserves both fulfillment and decisive endpoint without claiming the law was pointless.
Mouth and heart belong to one confession-and-belief description; the sequence is not presented as a mechanical formula.
The Greek can ask how people believe in one ‘whom they have not heard,’ allowing Christ to be the heard speaker, not merely the topic of a message.
The pinned source reads ‘the word of Christ’; some manuscripts read ‘the word of God.’
Gentile believers are pictured as a wild shoot grafted among Israel's branches. The root supports them, and the warning explicitly rules out boasting over the branches.
‘All Israel’ and ‘in this way’ have several substantial interpretations. The main text preserves Paul's wording without identifying Israel with one later theory.
‘Enemies’ describes a relation ‘with respect to the gospel’ in Paul's argument; the same people remain beloved with respect to election.
The two occurrences of ‘everyone’ are retained: all are confined in disobedience so that God may show mercy to all.
vocabulary: Graft a shoot into a tree.
A divine purpose once hidden and now disclosed.

notes: The whole embodied life is pictured as a living sacrifice; the image is not reduced to inward devotion.
‘The lowly’ may refer to humble people or humble tasks. The main text leaves the referent open.
The reader is forbidden personal vengeance and commanded to feed an enemy. The burning-coals image is retained without turning care into disguised retaliation.

Paul's statements about governing authority, judgment, taxation, and the sword are translated as written. The main text does not insert a modern political theory or claim that every ruler's conduct is good.
The sword represents real coercive and potentially lethal force; it is not softened to a vague symbol.
Love fulfills the law by refusing harm to the neighbor; the continuing debt of love remains owed.
‘Weapons of light’ preserves the military term also translated ‘instruments’ in Romans 6.
vocabulary: Authority, ruling power, or right to act.

notes: The ‘weak’ and ‘strong’ language belongs to Paul's argument about food and days. Both groups are commanded to stop despising or judging those God has welcomed.
The pinned Greek reads ‘God's judgment seat’; some witnesses read ‘Christ's judgment seat.’
Paul calls food clean while treating injury to another person's conscience as serious. Personal liberty does not cancel responsibility for another.
The bracketed words ‘be ensnared or become weak’ are present in the pinned main text and are retained.
vocabulary: A stumbling block or cause of falling.

notes: The strong are told to bear the weaknesses of others and follow Christ's self-denial; welcome is mutual rather than assimilation into one group's preferences.
Paul uses priestly language for his Gentile mission: he performs sacred service so that the Gentiles themselves become an offering made holy by the Spirit.
Spain is Paul's intended destination, with Rome as a visit and support point; the verse does not say the journey was completed.
The material contribution is described both as voluntary delight and as a debt arising from shared spiritual blessings.
Paul names danger from disobedient people in Judea and uncertainty about whether the Jerusalem saints will accept his service.
vocabulary: Bear, carry, or support a burden.
